GA004-020----:
On N-facing slope of a low rise in undulating grassland. An irregularly shaped standing stone of sandstone (H 1.6m). The numerous small depressions on its surface are probably due to erosion. A ringfort (GA044-019----) lies 135m to NW.

GA005-051----:
On SE-facing slopes of Slieve Dart overlooking gently undulating farmland. The monument consists of a pair of galleries set back to back and 1.75m apart. They are aligned roughly E-W and are incorporated in a cairn of uncertain outline (c. 22m E-W, c. 15m N-S). The E gallery (L 6.7m, Wth c. 1.5m), which consists of two chambers, is preceded by a short ante-chamber. In front, and to S of this, are the meagre remains of a court represented by two orthostats. The W gallery is poorly preserved; only its E end survives (L 2.5m, Wth c. 1.1m). There are no indications of a court at this end of the monument, (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1972, 1-2; Ó Nualláin 1989, 118)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. II - North Galway'. Compiled by Olive Alcock, Kathy de hÓra and Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1999).

In W half of an earthwork (GA006-001----). Named on 1st ed. of OS 6-inch map as 'Standing Stone' but on 3rd. ed. (1926) as 'Cloghmeel'. No visible surface trace survives. (Knight c. 1975, 110)

GA006-005001-:
On a tract of flat land in an area of gently sloping pasture. The tomb is eccentrically incorporated in a circular cairn (D c. 10m) which has been reused as a CBG (GA006-005----). A large roofstone rests above a collapsed chamber, aligned E-W, represented by at least four stones. The remains are insufficient to allow classification. (Melvin c. 1971, 8; Ó Nuallain 1989, 142)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. II - North Galway'. Compiled by Olive Alcock, Kathy de hÓra and Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1999).
Date of upload: 05 August 2010
GA006-125----:
In level grassland. An irregularly shaped pillar of eroded limestone (H 1.2m) leaning sharply to W. Around the base is a scatter of small stones used to secure it in an upright position. Presently used as a scratching stone, it also once acted as S pillar of a now disused gateway
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. II - North Galway'. Compiled by Olive Alcock, Kathy de hÓra and Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1999).
Date of upload: 05 August 2010
GA007-113----:
Located 4.5m NE of a ringfort (GA007-109----) is a rectangular limestone standing stone (H 1.54m) tapering slightly towards the top. Its long axis runs NE-SW.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. II - North Galway'. Compiled by Olive Alcock, Kathy de hÓra and Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1999).
Date of upload: 05 August 2010
GA009-002001-:
This monument is longitudinally incorporated in the possible remnants of the bank of a circular enclosure (GA009-002002-). It consists of a small narrow chamber (L >2m, Wth c. 0.7m) aligned E-W, formed by two sidestones and covered by a single roofstone. The tops of the sidestones slope down from W to E. A partially concealed stone to E may be a backstone. (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1972, 3-4)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).

GA009-005----:
On N side of a shallow valley 1.6km SE of Renvyle Point. The tomb consists of a gallery (L 4.2m) aligned NE-SW. Entrance to the gallery at NE is by two tall, well-matched portal stones. Little of S side of the gallery survives and N side is incorporated in a fence. The large slab lying within the gallery area and resting on N side may be a displaced roofstone. The monument is clearly of court/portal-tomb type and while it could well be a hybrid, the evidence, on balance, indicates close affinities with the court-tomb class, (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1972, 2-3)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).

GA009-010----:
On N side of a valley c. 3km SE of Renvyle. The monument is greatly disturbed and is partly incorporated in an animal pen. It comprises the ruins of a chamber aligned NW-SE. The entrance, at SE, is marked by a tall portal stone flanking a doorstone. A sidestone, partly overlapping the portal, leans out to SW and a large upright slab, probably a displaced roofstone, leans against it. A second flat roofstone, to NW, overlies another large slab. The NE side of the monument is missing; an old field fence abuts the entrance on this side. While the precise design cannot be established with certainty, the monument appears to be of the portal-tomb class.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).

GA009-021----:
On a gentle NW-facing slope at W end of Tully Mountain. This tomb comprises a gallery (L c. 5m, Wth c. 1.4m) aligned E-W and divided by jambs into two chambers. The entrance, at E, is marked by two portal stones. A displaced lintel lies immediately to W. Three large slabs, apparently displaced roofstones, rest against the gallery walls, (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1972, 4-5)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).

GA009-035----:
In very rough bogland at a break in slope on a S-facing slope. Tully Mountain is visible to the NE and Maumfin is to the SW. This standing stone consists of an irregular piece of white veined quartz (max. H 1.1m; max. Wth 1.1m) aligned NE-SW. The SW face, which is visible from the roadway to the SW, is roughly triangular in shape and varies in height from 1.1m at the SE end to 0.4m at the NW end. The NW side of the boulder is obscured with heather. Another standing stone (GA022-125----) lies c. 600m to the site.
The monument was brought to the attention of the Archaeological Survey of Ireland by Helen Riekstiņš.
Compiled by: Olive Alcock
Date of revised upload: 5 May 2017
GA010-003----:
On the level summit of The Tulach, a prominent ridge between Tully Mountain and Tully Lough. Known as Finn Mc Cool's Fingers, it comprises six stones, aligned N-S, and measuring 16m overall. The three northern stones are rounded granite boulders, decreasing in height from N to S (1.8m, 1.2m, 0.7m). The southern stones, which also decrease in height from N to S (1.6m, 0.7m, 0.5m), are, in contrast, rectangular slabs of schist. A possible seventh stone lies c. 0.6m further to N. The row is part of a complex of monuments on the hill which includes a pre-bog enclosure c. 100m to NE (GA010-005----), an unclassified stone structure c. 35m to SW (GA010-004----), and a series of pre-bog field walls (GA010-006----). (Killanin 1954, 98-9; Ó Nualláin 1988, 195; Gibbons and Higgins 1988a)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).
Date of upload: 05 August 2010
GA010-030----:
On flat, reclaimed bogland to ESE of Tully Cross. The monument, in ruins, consists of a gallery (L c. 3m, Wth c. 1.1m) aligned WNW-ESE. The W end of the gallery is closed by a large stone set outside the ends of the side-walls. An inclined stone of unknown function stands within the open E end of the gallery. Two large slabs, probably displaced roofstones, rest on the monument at NW. The remains are insufficient to permit classification.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).
Date of upload: 05 August 2010
GA011-002----:
On N side of Glencraff valley. The monument consists of a small wedge-shaped chamber, aligned E-W (L 1.75m, Wth 1m at the broader open, W end). It is formed of three stones and covered by a single roofstone which slopes down slightly from W to E. The remains can be interpreted as E end of a wedge-tomb.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).
Date of upload: 05 August 2010
GA011-009----:
Near the head of a valley 1.5km to S of, and overlooking the inner reaches of, Killary Harbour. The tomb consists of a gallery (L c. 2.4m, Wth 1.25m at the broader, open E end) aligned NE-SW. The W end is closed by a large stone set outside the line of the side-walls. A single stone exposed to SE of the gallery may indicate outer walling. A large slab in the chamber area may be a displaced roofstone. The monument cannot be classified with certainty but appears to be related to the wedge-tomb class. (Gibbons and Higgins 1988d, 65)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).

In gently undulating grassland. A tall irregular limestone slab (H 2m), subrectangular in plan, aligned E-W.

GA022-002----:
On the crown of a glacial ridge, incorporated into a modern field bank. Aligned NNE-SSW and c. 1.2m apart. Both stones are of granite. The N stone is subrectangular in plan (H 1.6m); S stone is now prostrate (1.4m by 0.65m). (Ó Nualláin 1988, 197)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).
Date of upload: 05 August 2010
GA022-006----:
On W side of a small valley overlooking Bundouglas Cove to N and Ballynakill Lough to SE. The monument is ruined and the remains comprise four stones. At E are two well-matched jambs which probably mark the entrance to a gallery. The other two stones form part of S side of the gallery. The remains are sufficient to indicate that the monument was a court-tomb (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1972, 7). This is one of a group of five tombs (GA022-007----, GA022-008----, GA022-063001-, GA022-106----) which, with a stone row (GA022-060----), a stone pair (GA022-009----); pre-bog field walls (GA022-077----) and several houses (GA022-113-----GA022-113007-), are centred on Lough Sheeauns c. 1km to SW. (Gibbons and Higgins 1988b; Molloy and O'Connell 1987)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).
Date of upload: 05 August 2010

GA022-007----:
On N side of the valley between Ballynakill Lough and Cleggan Bay. The remains of this tomb comprise a gallery (L c. 5m, Wth 1.5m) aligned ENE-WSW. The S side of the gallery is incorporated in a fence. At E are two fine entrance jambs. The gallery is divided into two chambers by a high sill, flanked by imbricated sidestones acting as jambs. The W portion of the inner, E chamber is covered by a large roofstone. Slight traces of a mound are visible immediately N of the gallery. See also GA022-006----. (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1972, 7-8)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).

GA022-008----:
Lower down and on N side of this valley and directly overlooking Lough Sheeauns. The remains comprise a ruined chamber (L c. 2m, Wth c. 1.3m) aligned roughly N-S; N end is incorporated in a roadside fence. A tall portal-like stone is embedded in the fence at NW. A displaced roofstone rests against E side. The tomb is very probably of the portal-tomb class. See also GA022-006----. (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1972, 8)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).

GA022-009----:
On a small hillock immediately to W of Ballynakill Lough. Aligned NW-SE and 3m apart. Both stones are of white quartz. The N stone is now prostrate (0.9m by 0.7m by 0.4m); S stone is pyramidal in 'shape (H 0.9m). Part of a complex of monuments centred on Lough Sheeauns to W (see GA022-006----). (Ó Nualláin 1988, 197, where misplaced in Sheeauns td.)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).
Date of upload: 05 August 2010
GA022-014----:
On N shore of Cleggan Bay. The remains of this tomb consist of a gallery aligned ESE-WNW. The front, E portion appears incomplete. The orthostats running E of the pair of transversely set jambs could be interpreted as chamber sidestones or as defining a narrow asymmetrical court. The gallery to W of these is divided into two chambers by a septal stone and jamb. The innermost W chamber is distinctly narrower and of lighter construction than the rest of the monument. A large roofstone covers the adjoining E chamber and a long stone, probably a displaced lintel, lies in this chamber immediately W of the jambs. The remains of the mound survive on S side of the monument. (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1972, 5-7)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).

GA022-015001-:
On a natural E-facing rise overlooking a stream. Pointed white quartz stone, rectangular in plan (H 1.4m). Possible house 17m to N (GA022-015002-) and a pre-bog wall (GA022-104----) to E on far side of stream.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).

GA022-019----:
On a low rise between Ballynakill Lough and Harbour. The monument consists of a small chamber (L c. 1.8m) covered by a roofstone. It is formed of two stones to N and a single stone to E. A small stone at W end does not appear to be in situ, and three other stones, probably outcropping rock, are exposed immediately SE of the chamber. Traces of a mound are visible around the structure. Though there is some doubt about the precise nature of the monument, it is clearly some form of burial chamber, (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1972, xxiii, n.1)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).
Date of upload: 05 August 2010
GA022-023----:
In pastureland just off the crest of a low ridge. Aligned N-S and 2m apart. Both stones are of granite and subrectangular in plan. The N stone is broken in two (H c. 1m); S stone (H 1.4m). There is a standing stone (GA022-099----) further downslope to SE (Ó Nualláin 1988, 197).
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).
Date of upload: 05 August 2010
GA022-028----:
Crowning a prominent hill. Revealed during recent turf-cutting and still partially buried in the bog. Aligned NE-SW and 2.7m apart. Both stones are of white quartz. The N stone is subrectangular in plan (H > 1m) and S stone, which is prostrate, is rectangular (H 1.65m). (Ó Nualláin 1988, 197)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).
Date of upload: 05 August 2010
GA022-030003-:
On a slight rise in cutaway bog, c. 40m to the SE of an enclosure (GA022-030002-). Aligned NW-SE and 1.8m apart. Both stones are of white quartz. The N stone is oval in plan (H 0.8m) and S stone is prostrate (1.3m by 0.75m). Another set stone lies 1.55m to SE but its relationship to the pair is unclear. It is rectangular in plan (H 0.4m). Both stones are clearly visible on current aerial imagery (OSi Digitalglobe 2011-2013; Geohive MapGenie Imagery 2013-2018). (Ó Nualláin 1988, 195)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).

GA022-036----:
Close to seashore on S side of Kingstown Bay. The remains of this partially ruined tomb are contained in a low oval mound (6m by 5.5m). The chamber (L 1.8m), aligned NW-SE, has been dug out and its S side is missing. It is formed by a single backstone to E and a double side-wall to N; a single stone, probable outer walling, is exposed to NW. The stones which formed its S side are probably among those which now lie along S edge of the mound. Although the remains cannot be classified with certainty, the tomb is very probably of the wedge-tomb class. (Petrie 1972, 253)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).
Date of upload: 05 August 2010
GA022-040----:
On the summit of a low hill in rough pastureland overlooking Garraunbaun Lough to the SW and Ballynakill Harbour to the N. This white quartz standing stone, rectangular in plan (H 1.55m; Wth 1.1m; T 0.8m), leans to the E. Grassed-over small granite boulders are visible at its base on the N and E sides. The standing stone is visible on current aerial imagery  (OSi digitalglobe 2011-2013). (Kinahan 1869c, 445, may be referring to it, amongst others;)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).

GA022-041----:
At the base of a steep N-facing hillslope to W of Ballynakill Harbour. The monument, very ruined, consists of a chamber (L 3m, Wth 1.1m), aligned NW-SE, with a very tall backstone at NW and transversely set jamb at SE. The remains are those of the rear chamber of a court-tomb. A pitched-out stone, 2m to SE of the chamber, may be a displaced entrance jamb. A large slab lies to N, beside the monument.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).
Date of upload: 05 August 2010
GA022-047----:
On the crown of a low ridge near W end of the peninsula forming N side of Clifden Bay. The remains of this ruined portal-tomb, which opens to SE, comprise three stones: N portal and adjoining sidestone and, to W, the backstone which leans inwards and rests on the sidestone. Traces of a low mound survive to N and W. (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1972, 9)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).

GA022-048----:
Close to the seashore on E side of Sellerna Bay. The monument consists of a small narrow chamber (L c. 2.3m, Wth c. 0.8m) aligned E-W, and covered by a roofstone supported at W by a large slab. The N and S sides are each formed of three stones. The sides extend beyond the single orthostat which closes E end. The monument is incorporated in a fence. The remains are insufficient to allow classification. (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1972, 5)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).

GA022-050----:
In pastureland on N side of Streamstown Bay. Described in 1872 as 'A remarkable, tall standing stone' (Kinahan 1872, 12) but apparently removed by time of 2nd ed. of OS 6-inch map (1898). However, Killanin (1954, 96) claimed that it still survived in early 1950s. No visible surface trace survives. (Killanin and Duignan 1967, 164)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).
Date of upload: 05 August 2010
GA022-051----:
On a S-facing slope overlooking Streamstown Bay. This tomb, fairly well preserved but lacking a roof, consists of a large single chamber (L 3.5m, Wth c. 1.7m) aligned NNW-SSE, with its rear set close to an escarpment of outcropping rock. The W side of the chamber is formed of three stones and the E side of two stones. The entrance, at S, is marked by two tall, well-matched portal stones set inside the line of the adjoining sidestones. A single set stone stands to S of W portal. Traces of a mound survive to S and W. While it can be classified as a portal-tomb, the possibility of it being the rear chamber of a court-tomb cannot be excluded.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).
Date of upload: 05 August 2010
GA022-060----:
On a low ridge overlooking Lough Sheeauns to N. Comprises three rounded granite stones, aligned NNW-SSE, and measuring c. 4.50m overall. The N stone (L 1.2m) has fallen, and centre stone (H 0.5m) is considerably smaller than S stone (H 1m). An outlying monolith of ?schist, with quartz inclusions, lies c. 7.5m NNW of the fallen N stone. Part of a complex of monuments centred on Lough Sheeauns (GA022-006----). (Ó Nualláin 1988, 195; Gibbons and Higgins 1988b)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).

GA022-063001-:
On a low hillock overlooking the inner end of Cleggan Bay to W. The monument, partly incorporated in a field wall, consists of a polygonal chamber (L c. 1.6m, Wth c. 1. 1m) open to NE and covered by a single roofstone. The chamber area has been dug out and the closing stone at SW may not be an original feature. The tomb is contained in a mound (6.5m by 5.5m). The remains are insufficient to permit classification. See also GA022-006----.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).

GA022-065----:
On the summit of a prominent bog-covered hill. Just visible on the surface of the bog is the top of what appears to be a white quartz standing stone. The stone pair on the hilltop in Crocknaraw (GA022-028----) is clearly visible to E.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).

GA022-067----:
On the summit of a hill overlooking the inner reaches of Streamstown Bay to SW. Two stones are aligned NE-SW and 1.75m apart. Both stones are of schist. The N stone is triangular in plan (H 1.1m) and S stone is rectangular (H 2.1m). A thin outlying monolith, irregular in plan (H 0.8m), lies 9m due SE of N stone. Lying beside it is another stone, also of schist (0.7m by 0.4m). Gibbons and Higgins (1988c) interpret this as a possible stone circle; it also has affinities with four-poster monuments. (Ormsby 1914; Kinahan 1872, 12; Ó Nualláin 1988, 197)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).

GA022-069001-:
At E end of a ridge overlooking the inner reaches of Streamstown Bay to S. This partially ruined tomb is incorporated in a mound (L 16m, Wth 12m). At E are remains of a court. The N arm is formed of three stones in line with the gallery side, and S arm is represented by a curved line of stones. The gallery, aligned ENE-WSW (L c. 6m, Wth c. 1.9m), is divided into two chambers by a pair of transversely set jambs; S side of E chamber is missing. The remains of a house (GA022-069003-) stand at N end of the mound. (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1972, 9-10)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).

GA022-072----:
On S-facing slope overlooking the inner reaches of Streamstown Bay. The monument consists of a subrectangular chamber (L 2.4m, Wth 1m) aligned ESE-WNW and closed at both ends by single slabs. A number of set stones to E and W of the monument appear to indicate further structure. Traces of a low mound are visible along W side. The chamber area has been completely dug out and the spoil deposited outside S side. The monument is clearly a megalithic tomb but the remains are insufficient to allow classification. (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1972, xxiii, n.1)

GA022-074----:
On low flat bogland between Ballynakill and Garraunbaun Loughs. The monument is very ruined and appears to be the last vestiges of a megalithic tomb. Several orthostats and a number of displaced stones appear to be the remains of a gallery, aligned N-S. The more southerly of the erect stones is a fine gable-shaped stone which may well be a backstone. (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1972, 8-9)

GA022-103001-:
On NW-facing slope overlooking Cleggan Bay. The monument is very ruined and comprises a gallery (L c. 7m) aligned NW-SE, divided into two chambers by a tall septal slab flanked by a jamb. Only W side of S chamber is exposed. The open, N chamber appears to have been dug out. A number of displaced roofstones lie along the gallery. A similar form of segmentation occurs at Cleggan (GA022-014----) and thus this monument can be assigned, with reasonable confidence, to the court-tomb class. Pre-bog field walls (GA022-103002-) occur to S and E. (Kinahan 1871, 350-1)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).
Date of upload: 05 August 2010
GA022-105----:
Just off the summit on NW slope of Ballynew hill. Incorporated into a modern field bank are two large thin quartz slabs, aligned NE-SW. The exact relationship of N stone (H 1.2m) to S stone (H 1.25m) is unclear as the latter may not be in situ There is also a pre-bog field system (GA022-089----) on this hill.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).
Date of upload: 05 August 2010
GA022-106----:
In a hollow to S of Lough Sheeauns. This tomb is very ruined. At E are the remains of a funnel-shaped court and 2m to W of this the rear chamber of the gallery (L 3m, Wth 1m). A large stone at the gallery entrance may be a displaced jamb. Traces of a low mound are visible to N and S of the monument and the remains of an old field wall survive to SW. See also GA022-006----.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).
Date of upload: 05 August 2010
GA022-107----:
In a relatively flat area of cutaway bog, now partly reclaimed, on N side of Ballynew hill. A thin and squat slab of schist, rectangular in plan (H 1m) with long axis running NNW-SSE. Leans heavily to SSE. Possibly a standing stone but could also be a remnant of the robbed pre-bog walls which lie c. 120m to E (GA022-089----):
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).
Date of upload: 05 August 2010
GA022-108----:
On the summit of a small hill. The edge of a thin slab (2m by 0.2m) is visible in the face of a turf cutting, covered by 0.3m of uncut bog. Possibly a prostrate standing stone.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).
Date of upload: 05 August 2010
GA022-115----:
On the shoreline of Knocknahaw townland, in an intertidal zone of Ballynakill Harbour. When first noted this possible stone row consisted of three granite boulders that were roughly evenly spaced and increased in height from W to E. However, while the morphology was typical of stone rows, the siting and orientation were atypical (information from M. Gibbons). Now only two boulders are clearly visible – the middle and outermost bolders. The innermost boulder is obscured by seaweed and boulders. It was not possible to measure the boulders as the tide was in.

In an area of rough grazing and gorse on an E-facing slope, overlooking Ballynakill Harbour with a panoramic view of the Twelve Bens from NE to SE. The view to the W is obscured by the growth of rhododendron. This standing stone (H 1m; Wth 1m; T 0.48m), aligned NW-SE, consists of a granite erratic. No packing stones are evident. The E face is flat while the W face is more rounded and uneven. It came to light in 2015 following the cutting back of the rhododendron, which is growing right up against the W face, and was brought to the attention of the Archaeological Survey of Ireland by Helen Riekstiņš. Another standing stone (GA009-035----) is visible c. 600m to the N.

GA023-008----:
On the summit of a low hillock overlooking Bearna Dhearg Bay to N. Rounded granite stone, oblong in plan (H 1.2m).

GA023-020----:
At W foot of Diamond Hill and within Connemara National Park. This tomb is very ruined and lacks a court. The remains consist of a gallery (L c. 5.5m) aligned N-S, divided into two chambers by a pair of transversely set jambs. There has been some interference with the structure at S end of the monument, and the stones here seem to represent the last vestiges of an old field wall. (Gibbons and Higgins 1988d, 65)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).
Date of upload: 05 August 2010
GA023-022----:
In a rocky defile to SE of Loch Ána. The monument is very ruined and is difficult to interpret. The remains of a possible chamber (L 2.5m, Wth c. 1.2m), opening to NE, can be distinguished among the rocks and boulders that litter the immediate area. It is possibly the remnants of a megalithic tomb.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).
Date of upload: 05 August 2010
GA023-024----:
On W-facing slope to S of Pollcappul Lough and within Connemara National Park. This ruined court-tomb is incorporated in a cairn (18m by 16m), which survives to a height of c. 1.5m. The remains comprise a gallery (L 6m, Wth c. 1.5m) aligned NE-SW. It is divided into two chambers by a single transversely set jamb; the SE side of the outer E chamber is concealed or missing. A fine entrance jamb survives at NE and the top of a possible court stone is exposed to E. The NE sector of the cairn is crossed by a path-like feature formed by the laying of a water pipe to a holy well (GA023-023001-) to SE of the monument. An old field wall abuts E corner of the cairn. (Gosling 1986, 47; Gibbons and Higgins 1988d, 65)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).
Date of upload: 05 August 2010
GA023-028----:
On the summit of a low hill overlooking the mouth of Abhainn an tSraithín. Thin slab of schist, rectangular in plan (H 1.63m) (GA023-028----). No visible trace survives of the faint 'rectangular enclosure [GA023-028001-], about 12ft. [3.65m] square' noted by Redington 'on the S side of this monument' (1914, 239-40). (Killanin 1954, 98)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).
Date of upload: 05 August 2010
GA023-029----:
Crowning the steep-sided promontory which divides Ballynakill Harbour from Bearna Dhearg Bay. Described by Redington (1914, 237) as 'an erratic boulder of white granite' (H c. 1.5m, L/Wth 0.85m). No visible trace of the stone (GA023-029----), or the small 'enclosure' (GA023-029001-) adjoining it on E (ibid., 239), survives; the promontory is now mantled by a fir plantation. A stone pair lies c. 250m to SSW (GA023-030----) and there is a pre-bog wall (GA023-039----) on SE slopes of the hill.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).
Date of upload: 05 August 2010
GA023-030----:
On the summit at S end of the promontory c. 250m SSW of GA023-029----. Aligned NNW-SSE and 2.6m apart. Both stones (GA023-030----) are of granite. The N stone is squat and subcircular in plan (H 0.5m); S stone is taller and oblong in plan (H 1.5m). No visible trace survives of the small 'enclosure' (GA023-030001-) noted by Redington (1914, 238-9) on E side of S stone.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).
Date of upload: 05 August 2010
GA023-031----:
On N-facing slope in cutaway bog overlooking Ballynakill Harbour to NW. Squat granite boulder, oval in plan (H 0.65m). Immediately to SE is a prostrate stone, partly obscured (> 1.55m by 0.55m). The standing stone in Roscrea (GA028-028----) is visible to W.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).
Date of upload: 05 August 2010
GA023-038----:
On the level summit of a prominent ridge. Three rounded granite stones aligned N-S, measuring 5.75m overall and decreasing in height from S to N. The N stone is oval in plan (H 0.85m), centre stone is subrectangular (H 0.9m) and S stone, which is shattered, was originally rectangular (H c. 1.5m).
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).
Date of upload: 05 August 2010
GA023-046----:
This stone pair is located in an area of rough grazing land on an E-W running ridge. It commands panoramic views overlooking Ballynakill Harbour and Tully Mountain to the NW. Diamond Hill and Doughruagh or Kylemore Mountain are visible to the E and NE respectively. The pair consists of two granite boulders, 2.3m apart, and while not parallel with one another, they lie on a roughly NNE-SSW axis. The taller boulder (H 1.32m; Wth 1.3m; T 0.85m), to the S, is flat-faced to the E and bears a more rounded profile to the W. The shorter N boulder (H 0.6m; L 1.2m; T 1m) is roughly trapezoidal in shape. The monument is obscured by the dense growth of cotoneaster, particularly around the S and W faces of the larger boulder. However, according to local information, it was clear of overgrowth in the mid-1960s, when it was visible as a more prominent feature in the landscape. This stone pair was brought to our attention by Helen Riekstiņš. Another example (GA023-030----) is known from this townland. It lies c. 225m to the NNW.

GA023-055----:
Located in Letterfrack National Park in an area of bogland on the SW slope of Diamond Hill and on the N bank of the Sruffaunnanoon river, close to its source; a small lake bed is visible to the W. There are clear views of the ocean further to the W and Bunowen Hill to the SW. This possible standing stone (H 1m; Wth 0.41m; T 0.3m), of local stone with quartz veins, is rectangular in plan. Moss and lichen are visible on it and its lower section is obscured by heather. This monument was brought to the attention of the Archaeological Survey of Ireland by Helen Riekstiņš.
Compiled by: Olive Alcock with information supplied by Helen Riekstiņš
Date of upload: 12 June 2019

The stones appear to define the ‘pier stones’ of a gateway and one of them may have been moved to its present position. This monument was brought to the attention of the Archaeological Survey of Ireland by Helen Riekstiņš.

This standing stone was discoverd by Mr. Colm Mac Diarmada (pers. comm. December 2014). It is in an upland area of rough grazing and cut-away bogland on a plateau on the SW hillslope of Binn Shléibhe/Ben Levy, overlooking Lough Corrib to the S. There are panoramic views from E through S to NW.
The standing stone is a conglomerate boulder (H 1m; base Wth 0.58m; max. Wth 1.15m; T 0.64m) which is roughly lozenge shaped – the flat surfaces face towards NW and SE. It is sitting on a small mound that is the result of bog being cut away. An area (Wth 0.5m; D 0.2m) around the  base of the stone has been poached away. Packing stones are evident.  A ring-barrow (GA026-020----) lies c. 260m to the NNW.

GA027-039----:
In limestone cragland just beyond S rim of a little valley, in an area now covered by a large plantation of conifers. The monument, fairly well preserved but concealed by cairn material, is aligned E-W. At E is part of N side of a court and a single stone of S side. Behind these is a gallery (L 4.2m), divided into two chambers. Corbelling is well preserved along both sides of the rear chamber and extends E into front chamber where it is obscured by debris. Two large broken roofstones rest above the corbelling and a massive lintel lies across the gallery entrance. The cairn is roughly oval in plan (L 15m, Wth 12m, H c. 2m) and envelops the gallery to level of roofstones, as well as apparently concealing the greater part of the court, (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1972, 10-11)

It consists of a roughly angled structure (L 3m, Wth 0.9m), aligned approximately ENE-WSW, and covered by two roof-stones. The W opening is divided by a longitudinally set stone. Traces of a mound are visible on W, N and E. The remains of this tomb are insufficient to permit classification. (Petrie 1972, 253, 'Dunmore, and a cromleac adjoining' may refer: see GA035-035001-)

On the shoreline in a boggy area on inner reaches of Streamstown Bay. Rounded granite stone, subrectangular in plan (H 1.6m).

On a slight rise in grassland. Marked on 3rd ed. of OS 6-inch map (1920) as three small dots aligned NE-SW. It consists two large eroded limestone slabs aligned as on map and set 2.2m apart. An unclassified stone structure (GA042-011----) lay 325m to S.

GA042-167003-:
Some 7m E of a ringfort (GA042-167001-) A tall thin slab of limestone conglomerate (H 2.05m), rectangular in plan, its long axis running N-S. It appears to be held in position by basal-packing stones, though field-clearance rubble has also been dumped against its base. (Killanin and Duignan 1967, 304-5)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. II - North Galway'. Compiled by Olive Alcock, Kathy de hÓra and Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1999).

GA051-013----:
On SW slopes of Cashel Hill. The monument is well preserved, consisting of a gallery aligned E-W (L 3.1m, Wth 1.2m at the broader W end). A transverse slab, leaning heavily outwards, separates the main chamber and portico. The former (L 1.7m) is roofed by a single slab. Closely set outer walling tapers to a point c. 1.5m E of the gallery's backstone. Traces of a mound survive around the monument. (Cooney 1986)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).
Date of upload: 05 August 2010
GA052-007----:
Crowning a prominent glacial ridge at the foot of Cnoc Úraid. Incorporated into a modern L-shaped sheepfold. Aligned N-S and c. 1.15m apart. Both stones are subrectangular in plan. The N stone is prostrate (1.14m by 0.65m by 0.55m); S stone (H 1.15m). A house lies 175m to SW (GA052-006----). (Ó Nualláin 1988, 197, who interprets it as 'two uprights and a prostrate stone')
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).
Date of upload: 05 August 2010
GA054-001----:
On an E-facing slope in pastureland. This standing stone (H 1.93m) consists of an irregular limestone slab that is leaning slightly southwards. The base (Wth 0.35m) is subrectangular in plan and the slab tapers towards the top (Wth 0.23m) where it sub-triangular in plan.
Compiled by: Olive Alcock
Date of upload: 10 November 2017
GA055-034----:
On a low knoll amidst gently rolling pasture, 1.2km from E shores of Lough Corrib. The monument is very ruined. It consists of a gallery (L 5.5m), aligned roughly E-W, represented by two entrance jambs at E, two sidestones on N and a backstone at W. A single courtstone flanks N jamb, and a stone in a similar position adjoining the opposite jamb may also be a courtstone. The overall length of the gallery would indicate that it had at least two chambers. The structure is incorporated in a subrectangular mound (L 12.5m, Wth 10m). There is an unclassified megalithic tomb (GA055-070----) c. 130m to NW and an anomalous stone group (GA055-069----) c. 160m to NNW. (Aldridge 1965, 15; de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1972, 12; Ó Nualláin 1989, 118)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. II - North Galway'. Compiled by Olive Alcock, Kathy de hÓra and Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1999).
Date of upload: 05 August 2010

GA055-069----:
On S-facing slope of a low hill in gently rolling pasture. It comprises a gallery (L c. 2.2m, Wth 1.75m), aligned E-W, represented by two stones on N side, one on S and a tall backstone (H 1.8m) at W. There is an upright stone at E which appears to have been displaced from the tomb. A large displaced stone protrudes from the field stones which fill the chamber. The remains are incorporated into a field wall beside an outhouse. A court tomb (GA055-034----) stands c. 130m to SE. (Aldridge 1965, 15)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. II - North Galway'. Compiled by Olive Alcock, Kathy de hÓra and Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1999).
Date of upload: 05 August 2010
GA056-054002-:
Some 35m SE of Cloghanover Castle (GA056-054001-). It comprises a squat limestone boulder (L 0.6m, Wth 0.35m, H 0.6m), its long axis running NW-SE. According to OS Letters (O'Flanagan 1927, Vol. 1, 187), this stone is known locally as 'Cloch an Uabhair'. It is reputed 'to have been cast hither from a distant hill by a witch called Cailleach an Uabhair who impressed the marks of her thumb and three fingers in it' (ibid.). Two other similar boulders are also visible in the vicinity of the castle, 1m to W and 40m to NNE respectively.
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. II - North Galway'. Compiled by Olive Alcock, Kathy de hÓra and Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1999).
Date of upload: 05 August 2010
GA056-147----:
Situated on top of a low rise in undulating pastureland. This large tapering slightly rounded limestone slab (H 1.85m; base Wth c. 1.35m; Wth at top 0.85m; T 0.5m) is aligned N-S. A number of small packing stones are visible around its base, particularly on its W side.

GA058-043----:
In a broad valley near W end of an isolated terrace of cragland, 1.6km S of Knockroe Hill. The monument, extant in 1960, has since been destroyed and no visible surface trace survives. It consisted of a long narrow gallery (L 8.2m, Wth 1.9m at W, narrowing to 1m at E), aligned roughly E-W. Five displaced slabs lay along it; these may have been fragments of the roof. The N side was represented by five orthostats and S side by seven; a backstone was in position at E end. Two outer wall-stones were exposed on N side and two on S side. The tomb was incorporated in a subrectangular mound (L 13, Wth < 8m). (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1972, 12-13; 6 Nualláin 1989, 137)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. II - North Galway'. Compiled by Olive Alcock, Kathy de hÓra and Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1999).

GA059-018----:
In flat pasture. The tomb comprises the remains of a ruined gallery (L 5.5, Wth c 2m), aligned NW-SE. Its overall length would indicate that it had at least two chambers. Four sidestones are present on N and two on S side of the gallery, and a backstone stands at its NW end. Finally, a single corbel or displaced roofstone protrudes from the ground at S side of the gallery. The structure is incorporated at SE end of a long low mound (L 27.5m, Wth 12m at SE, narrowing to c. 3m at NW). (Ó Nualláin 1989, 118)

On gently sloping pakureland some 70m E of the Killaclogher River. The remains comprise a ruined gallery (L 2.4m, Wth 1.2m), aligned ENE-WSW, represented by three stones on N and two on S side which support a single roofstone. Although the monument cannot be classified with certainty, interpretation as a wedge-tomb would not be inconsistent with the present remains. (Claffey 1983, 154-6; Ó Nualláin 1989, 137)

On grassy limestone close to the shore of Lough Corrib. The monument is fairly well preserved but lacks a roof. It consists of a chamber (L c. 4m, Wth 1.5m) aligned E-W, formed by two portal stones, at E, and two sidestones; N portal is flanked by an orthostat. The tomb is incorporated in a cairn of irregular outline. The S side of the chamber forms part of a field wall. (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1972, 13)

GA094-012----:
In a shallow valley at the head of Leckanaloy Creek, c. 100m from the seashore. Described by de Valera and Ó Nualláin (1972, 14) as a small chamber (L 2.5m, Wth c. 1.8m), aligned ESE-WNW, composed of two portal-stones at E, a backstone at W and N sidestone. The S portal leans markedly outwards and a large displaced roofstone lies across the chamber. The remains of a small earthen enclosure (3m by 2.5m) abut its N side. Fragments of cremated bone and sherds of coarse pottery were recovered from the chamber. (McCaffrey 1952, 9; Waddell 1977, 58-9)

GA095-078----:
In flat pastureland with outcropping rock, c. 450m to the SE of the Clarinbridge River. This tomb is now in ruins having collapsed c. 1930. Westropp's (1901, 438) account indicates that it comprised a roughly wedge-shaped chamber (L c. 2.5m; Wth 1.4m at W narrowing to 1.3m at E), aligned E-W, formed of two stones at N and one stone at S, which supported a large roofstone. It would seem probable that the monument was a wedge-tomb. (McCaffrey 1952, 10-11, 135; de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1972, 14-15)
See linked document with details from Ruaidhrí de Valera and Seán Ó Nualláin, Survey of the Megalithic Tombs of Ireland. Volume III. Counties Galway, Roscommon, Leitrim, Longford, Westmeath, Laoighis, Offaly, Kildare, Cavan. (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1972).

GA095-119----:
In pastureland with outcropping rock, some 350m to the S of the seashore at the inner reaches of Mweeloon Bay. This tomb comprised the ruins of a gallery (L 5.5m), aligned NW-SE, divided into two chambers by a sill-stone. The entrance, at SE, was between two jambs; the N jamb was flanked by a single courtstone. A large displaced stone, possibly a roofstone, lay in the front chamber. The tomb was bulldozed during the course of land clearance in 1964. The orthostats were pushed to the fence at the N boundary of the field. (Holt 1912, 249-50; McCaffrey 1952, 11-12; de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1972, 15-16)

GA097-150005-:

On a hummock in grassland, in the former Ballydonnellan estate. A limestone slab (H 1.3m), roughly rectangular in plan, aligned NE-SW. Now used as a scratching stone.

GA098-067----:

GA098-067001-:

GA102-041----:
On Tawin Island, in grazing land close to the foreshore. Holt (1911-12, 249) recorded a slight elevation that was partly enclosed by the arms of a large shallow pool, and on which there were a number of granite boulders that may have formed part of an irregular stone circle. He was informed that 'the appearance of a circle was more marked, before other boulders of the series were broken up for building.' On inspection in May 1992, five irregularly shaped granite boulders (max. H 1.7m; Wth 2.4m; T 1.8m) enclosed a roughly oval area (30m NE-SW; 26m NW-SE); a slight depression in the interior at N may have marked the socket of a boulder that had been removed. Two of the boulders were recumbent but one of them was not set into the ground; one other boulder also did not appear to be set. On re-inspection in May 2008 no visible surface trace of the boulders survived. According to local information, large boulders were removed from this area in the late 1990s to build up coastal defences along the shoreline to the N. Not precisely located.
Compiled by: Olive Alcock
Date of upload: 13 December 2019
GA103-004----:
Close to the summit of a low ridge overlooking marshland to the SW. This standing stone (H 1.5m; base Wth 1.15-1.2m narrowing to 0.37-1m at top) consists of a granite slab, roughly rectangular in plan and leaning to the SW. Partly displaced, it is aligned NE-SW. (Gosling 1986, 17)
Compiled by: Galway Archaeological Survey, UCG
Date of upload: 13 December 2019
GA103-027----:
In undulating pastureland. This standing stone consists of a limestone slab (H 2.3m; Wth 1.4m), rectangular in plan and aligned NW-SE. The base of the stone is 0.58m thick but on the SW face, at a height of 0.6m from ground level, it narrows to 0.35m where a natural ledge formation occurs. (McCaffrey 1952, 180, no. 8)

GA104-034----:

GA104-035----:
On a N-facing downslope in pastureland. This standing stone consists of a karstic limestone slab with evidence of water channels. It is rectangular in plan (H 2.7m; max. Wth 1.83m), tapering towards the top (Wth 0.6m). It is aligned NNW-SSE and leans towards the W. Some field stones are piled against the base on the W side. Lichen is visible on all faces of the stone and it is used as a scratching post by livestock. A structural crack is evident towards the lower end of the E face. (McCaffrey 1952, 213, no. 68)
Compiled by: Olive Alcock

GA104-273----:
On a low knoll near the W end of a long ridge in rolling farmland, some 3.5km to the SE of Craughwell. Described by de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1(972, 16-17) as the remains of a long gallery (L > 9m; Wth 1.9m at W narrowing to 0.9m near E end), aligned ENE-WSW, flanked along either side by outer-walling. A high septal-stone at W separated a short portico (L 1.6m) from the remainder of the gallery (L c. 7m). A single displaced roofstone lay across the middle of the gallery. The structure is incorporated in an irregularly shaped mound. On re-inspection in December 2007 the monument was heavily overgrown and field-clearance material had been dumped around its perimeter. (McCaffrey 1952, 14)

GA105-162----:
On a ridge in pastureland, immediately to the S of the Loughrea-Portumna road. Named the ‘Seven Monuments’ and shown within a large mixed forest on the OS 6-inch maps, this National Monument was known locally as 'Feara Breige'. It was described in Dutton’s Statistical Survey of 1824 as a mound where there were ‘formerly eight flat rude stones’, but one was missing, five were still standing and two were lying flat on the bank. In the centre was a ‘tumulus’ and the entire site was planted with trees (O'Flanagan 1927, Vol. 2, 239). The trees have since been removed from the monument but traces of the plantation survive immediately to its S and around its W limits and a house has been built to its SE. Traces of lazy beds, running roughly NE-SW are visible immediately to its S. This embanked stone circle (30.15m N-S) is defined by a raised roughly circular area that is enclosed by a well-preserved mainly earthen flat-topped bank (Wth at N 0.8m; int. H 0.5m; ext. H 0.8m) that is clearly visible all round. An outhouse built in the early 1980s clips it a SE (SMR file). There is small gap (base Wth 0.7m) in the bank at SE. The seven boulders are still extant: two at NW and N are lying flat and the other five at NE, E, SE, SSE and SSW are upright. Within the interior, roughly centrally located, is a small cairn (1.8m N-S; H 0.35-0.7m). A low berm (Wth 11.7m) visible around it slopes gently towards the bank. There is no visible surface trace of a fosse. Knox (1915, 310-11) recorded traces of an outer bank to the N, E and S. It is now only clearly visible from N to NE (L c. 16.4m; Wth 0.5m; int. H 1.7m; ext. H 1m). Here a field wall is built outside it and there is a sharp drop (H 1.8m) to the road below. Otherwise only slight intermittent traces are evident from SW to N and this area is densely overgrown with scrub and trees. Knox (1915-16, 72) suggested that the central cairn was possibly an Ordnance Survey station and an excavation by Macalister (1916-17, 506-7), which proved that it was of recent origin, may back this up. The upstanding stones range in height from 1.08m to 1.56m and packing stones are visible at the base of some. Most are partially covered with moss and lichen. The top of the stone (L c. 0.2m; Wth 0.2m) at WSW is fairly flat and bears a roughly square tenon-like feature (H 0.02m; L 0.05m; Wth 0.05m), again suggesting a possible link with an OS trigonometrical station.

GA105-237----:
Located on a prominent hillock on a NE-SW running ridge, this standing stone (H 0.8m; c 0.55m x 0.24m) is aligned N-S and is embedded in a stony base. It is known locally as the ‘Lady Stone’ or the ‘Earl’s Chair’ and it is believed that Nora Novar, who reputedly built the townland boundary wall, is buried here. The standing stone was identified by Dr F. Beglane (pers. comm. November 2014). Ringforts (GA105-081---- and GA105-080----) are visible c. 135m to the NNW and c. 455m to the NNE respectively, and all the monuments lie within the N half of a medieval deerpark (GA105-236----). (Beglane 2014, 315)

GA110-053----:
In the area of Inis Mór called Fearann an Choirce, on a level limestone pavement overlooking seashore to N. The monument, in ruins, consists of a slightly wedge-shaped gallery, aligned E-W, represented by two opposed sidestones (L 3.5m, Wth 1.5m at W end narrowing to 1.2m at E). A single outer wall stone survives to S. A jamb-like stone stands within the gallery at W end and 0.6m further W are two façade stones incorporated in a field wall. A large slab lying N of the gallery, and partly covered by the wall, may be a displaced roofstone. Slight traces of a mound are visible to N and S of the tomb. (O'Flanagan 1927a, Vol. 3, 268; Westropp 1895, 266)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).
Date of upload: 05 August 2010
GA110-098----:
At W end of the central ridge of Inis Mór, in the subdivision known as Corruch. The tomb is fairly well preserved and is a Nat. Mon. It consists of a wedge-shaped gallery, aligned ENE-WSW (L 2.5m, Wth 1.8m at the open W end narrowing to 0.8m at the rear which is closed by a single slab). A closely set double wall of slabs runs along the exterior of S side. The gallery is roofed by three overlapping slabs. Some slight traces of a mound are apparent to S of the monument. (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1972, 17-18; Robinson 1980)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).

GA112-009----:
In pastureland with outcropping rock, some 500m to the S of Kinvarra Bay. The tomb consists of a simple wedge-shaped chamber (L 2.5m; Wth 1.5m at SW narrowing to 1.2m at NE) formed of three uprights and open to the SW. It is covered by a single roofstone on top of which is piled a stack of field stones. The chamber decreases in height from SW to NE and is surrounded by a low mound. (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1972, 24-5; Korff and O'Connell, 1985)

GA114-100003-:
Associated with a rath (GA114-100001-). According to a field report in 1970 (SMR file), there were 'two standing stones near the edge of [this] fort (one c. 6' [1.8m] high)'. Only one quartz pillar stone (H 1.9m; Wth 0.87m; T 0.67m) is now visible in the E sector of the interior of the rath. Traces of packing stones are evident around its base. No trace of the second stone survives. Possibly a stone pair originally?

GA115-014----:
On level pastureland, immediately to to the S of a small stream. This megalithic tomb consists of a chamber (L 2.5m; Wth 1.3m) aligned NW-SE. It is formed by a backstone at E, two sidestones at S, a single sidestone at N, and a high septal-stone at W. The chamber is filled with field stones. The remains of another wedge tomb (GA115-015----) stand c. 120m to the ENE.
Compiled by: Galway Archaeological Survey, UCG
Date of upload: 19 August 2019
GA115-015----:
Some 120m to the ENE of another wedge tomb (GA115-014----). This tomb comprises a low mound (diam. c. 4m) along the perimeter of which are three outward-leaning slabs at N and a single set stone at S: these are aligned E-W. Four other stones protrude from the mound and a large slab lies to NW. The stones along the perimeter could be interpreted as the remains of the outer-walling of the wedge tomb.
Compiled by: Galway Archaeological Survey, UCG
Date of upload: 19 August 2019
GA116-018----:
In gently undulating pastureland. Indicated and named 'Stone' in Roman script on the 1838 edition of the OS 6-inch map. No visible surface trace survives. A limekiln has been built here. The landowner did not recall there being a monument here. Possibly the site of a standing stone.

On inspection all that was visible was a small stone, which was irregular in shape and only a few centimetres above the ground surface. In gently rolling farmland, some 4km to the NW of Portumna. Overgrown with thorn and bramble, this tomb has been used as a dump for field stones. The remains comprise a gallery (L 4m; Wth 1m), aligned approximately E-W, represented by three stones at N and two at S. Two outer-wall stones stand to the S of the gallery and a displaced slab lies at its W end. The structure is embedded in a mound (L 12m; Wth 8m
average). (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1972, 18–19)

On a rise in hilly grassland. Marked on the 1838 edition of the OS 6-inch map as a subcircular enclosure (c. 70m N-S; c. 68m E-W) clipped by a N-S running field boundary at NNE and SSE; partially levelled by the time of the 1947 edition. All that survives is the arc of a low bank from W to N, directly inside of which is a shallow but wide fosse (Wth 4m); otherwise no visible surface trace survives. A children's burial ground  (GA117-049001-) lies within SE sector of the interior.

GA119-036----:
Close to the edge of a limestone terrace above the sea on W side of Inis Meáin. The monument is very ruined. The gallery (L c. 3m), aligned E-W, is represented by one N sidestone, now markedly pitched to S, and two S sidestones, lying flat beneath a large displaced roofstone. A number of displaced slabs cover W end of the gallery. Some slight traces of a cairn are apparent around the tomb which seems to have been built on bare rock. (Robinson 1980)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).

GA119-077----:
On Inis Meáin, in an area of small pasture fields to NNE of and below Baile an Mhothair. No trace of this monument survives. In 1839 it consisted of a chamber formed by two sidestones, each about 3.25m long, and a partly displaced slab which closed SE end; N end was open. A single horizontal roofstone rested on the sidestones. The description suggests a simple wedge-tomb. (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1972, 27)
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Galway Vol. I - West Galway'. Compiled by Paul Gosling (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1993).

GA119-078----:
On Inis Meáin, on bare flat limestone cragland to NE of and below Baile an Mhothair. This Nat. Mon., known locally as Leaba Dhiarmada 'is Ghrainne, is very ruined. The gallery (L c. 3.5m), aligned E-W, is represented by two large sidestones now pitched markedly to S beneath a large roofstone. Outer walling occurs to N and S of the gallery. A displaced upright stone at W end of the gallery may have formed part of an entrance feature. Some slight traces of cairn survive around the tomb which appears to have been built directly on bare rock, (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1972, 18-19; Robinson 1980)

GA120-020----:
In a level area of small fields on W side of the island. The remains consist of a slightly wedge-shaped gallery opening to SE (L 3.5m, Wth 1.75m at NW narrowing to 1.3m at SE). GA122-019----:
On flat pastureland, c. 1.2km to the NW of Coole Lough. The megalithic tomb consists of a wedge-shaped chamber (L > 4.5m; Wth 2m at W narrowing to 1.2m at E), aligned NE-SW, which is incorporated in an oval mound. The chamber sides, each of one great slab, decrease in height from W to E and support a massive roofstone. Both ends of the tomb are blocked by modern drystone walls. Two closely set outer-wall stones are exposed beside the S sidestone. Some 2m to the SW of the chamber are two stones, which may be the remains of a flat façade. (Killanin and Duignan 1967, 300; de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1972, 19-20)

GA125-119----:
This is one of a group of three tombs (see also GA125-121---- and GA125-128----), which are situated on rolling farmland, c. 1km to the NW of Ballinlough in the NE foothills of the Slieve Aughty Mountains. This tomb comprises a ruined chamber (L c. 2m), with the entrance at SE, formed of two portal-stones and two sidestones above which rests a large roofstone: the E portal-stone and sidestone have collapsed inwards. A displaced stone lies immediately in front of the entrance and two others occupy the N end of the chamber. Traces of a low mound are discernible around the tomb. Marble Hill demesne, within which this monument formerly stood, also contained four other megalithic-type structures: see GA125-120----, GA125-123----, GA125-130---- and GA125-131----. (O'Flanagan 1927, Vol. 3 522; de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1972, 21)

GA125-121----:
In rolling hilly pastureland, some 210m to the S of a portal-tomb (GA125-119----). This tomb comprises the ruins of a long narrow gallery (L 10m) aligned NE-SW. A septal-stone at SW separates a short portico (L c. 1.4m) from the remainder of the gallery (L 7.2m) of which six sidestones are in position at N, five at S, and a backstone at E. Two roofstones rest in a sloping position above the gallery walls. A single upright stone at N forms a doubling of the wall and a line of five stones to the S of the gallery may be the remains of an outer wall. The gallery is incorporated in an irregularly shaped mound on which lie a number of displaced slabs. (O'Flanagan 1927, Vol. 3 22; de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1972, 21-2)

The remains comprise a short wedge-shaped gallery (L c. 3m; Wth estimated c. 1.5m at W narrowing to c. 1m at E), aligned E-W, represented by a closing stone at E, a single sidestone at N, two sidestones at S, and a backstone at E. On an E-facing slope in the grounds of Cloonmoylan House. Known locally as the ‘Druid's Altar’, this upright inverted T-shaped undressed slab (H 2.16m; base Wth 0.96m; Wth at top 0.45m; T 0.09m) is aligned N-S. Possibly a standing stone but it may also be a folly.

GA128-061----:
On a NW-facing slope in an area of pastureland and outcropping rock. This standing stone is now recumbent. It consists of a large prostrate undressed subrectangular stone (L c. 1.9m) which tapers towards the S end It is partially covered by a small cairn of field-clearance boulders.

GA129-011----:
In gently rolling pastureland, overlooking Ballynakill Lough some 400m to the N. This tomb consists of a small wedge-shaped chamber (L 2m; Wth c. 1.8m at SW narrowing to 1.4m at NE), aligned NE-SW, decreasing in height from W to E. The chamber, closed at SW by a single slab, is covered by a roofstone. Outer-walling survives to the S, and especially around the NE end. It is incorporated in a small mound which rises almost to roof height. (Killanin and Duignan 1967, 300; de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1972, 23-4)

GA129-018----:
On low ground in undulating farmland, c. 200m to the SE  of a small stream. This tomb consists of a wedge-shaped chamber (L c. 3.5m; Wth 1.6m at W narrowing to 1.3m at E), aligned ENE-WSW, formed by a single sidestone at N and two sidestones at S which support a large roofstone. Traces of a low mound are present at N and W. (Killanin and Duignan 1967, 300; de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1972, 23)

GA129-038----:
On a fairly steep S-facing slope, near the base of a narrow pasture ridge. This standing stone, comprising  a piece of karst limestone pavement (L 1.5m; Wth 0.6m at NNE end, narrowing to 0.45m at SSW end) that has been set on edge, is orientated NNE-SSW. It is roughly rectangular in plan but L-shaped in profile and is 1.45m in maximum height at its NNE end. At its lower SSW end it is only 0.5m high. A number of solution holes are evident on the stone. One small boulder at the base of the stone on its E side may be a packing stone. Loose stones on its W side may be the result of field clearance. Lichen covers all faces of the stone and the NNE is smooth as a result of cattle rubbing against it.
